extracted.intended_audience: inventors, patent applicants, patent prosecutors, and in-house counsel
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on how the transitional phrase in a patent claim (preamble/transitional/body) affects claim scope and infringement analysis, and when to use 'comprising', 'consisting of', or 'consisting essentially of'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim sections and their roles
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent claim has three major sections, namely, a preamble, a transitional phrase, and a body. The body of the claim contains the elements which define the scope of patent protection as defined by that claim. The transitional phrase indicates whether incorporating other elements or components in an accused infringing device other than those elements recited in the body would avoid infringement of the claim. The preamble in general defines the environment (i.e., context) of the claimed invention but does not limit the claim unless the preamble breathes life into the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this structure to reason about scope: the 'body' lists limitations that must be present; the 'transitional phrase' controls whether additional, unrecited elements exclude infringement; treat the preamble as non-limiting unless it supplies essential limitations ('breathes life').

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of 'comprising' (open transitional phrase)
rubrics_metrics.description: The transitional phrase 'comprising' is referred to as an open transitional phrase because even if the accused infringing device includes additional components and elements, the accused infringing device will not avoid infringement as long as the accused infringing device incorporates all of the elements recited in the body of the claims or the claim elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer 'comprising' in most patent claims to retain an open-ended scope and avoid loss of infringement simply because an accused product has extra components. The article advises that 'in the vast majority of patent cases, the claims should utilize the open transitional phrase "comprising"' to avoid issues raised by closed forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of 'consisting of' (closed transitional phrase)
rubrics_metrics.description: The transitional phrase 'consisting of' is referred to as a closed transitional phrase. When a claim's transitional phrase is 'consisting of,' adding an additional component or element to the accused infringing device may avoid infringement of the claim even if the accused infringing device incorporates all of the limitations and elements recited in the body of the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For a claim with the 'consisting of' transitional phrase, if an added element is related to the invention then the accused infringing device does not infringe the claim. Case examples: Norian (spatula unrelated—court held accused product infringed despite additional element) and Shire Development (added lipophilic substance related—Federal Circuit held no infringement). Be cautious: using 'consisting of' can narrow scope and produce unexpected non-infringement depending on whether added elements are related to the invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of 'consisting essentially of' (partially closed transitional phrase)
rubrics_metrics.description: The transitional phrase 'consisting essentially of' is referred to as a partially closed transitional phrase. If the accused infringing device includes an added component or element that materially affects the basic and novel characteristic of the invention, then the accused infringing device does not infringe the claimed invention. If the added component does not materially affect the basic and novel characteristic of the invention and affects it only in a minor way, then the accused infringing device would still infringe the patent claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain the distinction between 'consisting of' and 'consisting essentially of': the latter permits additions that do not materially affect the invention's basic and novel characteristic, while excluding those that do. Courts guard this distinction and resist reading 'consisting of' as equivalent to the partially closed form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial precedent and MPEP govern interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Judicial decisions (e.g., Shire Development LLC v. Watson Pharmaceuticals, Inc.; Norian) and the Manual of Patent Examining Procedure (MPEP § 2111.03) provide detailed explanations and govern how transitional phrases are interpreted for claim scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or drafting claims, consult MPEP guidance and relevant case law because courts compare precedent (Norian vs. later cases like Shire) to determine whether added elements fall within or outside a closed/partially closed transitional phrase. Specific facts (e.g., whether an added element is related to the invention or materially affects a characteristic) drive outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical drafting/prosecution guidance: prefer open but consider closed forms strategically
rubrics_metrics.description: For the layperson, in the vast majority of patent cases, the claims should utilize the open transitional phrase 'comprising' which is open-ended and avoids this issue altogether. However, during examination or patent prosecution, there may be times when utilizing the 'consisting essentially of' or 'consisting of' transitional phrases may be useful in overcoming a rejection made by the examiner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before using 'consisting of' or 'consisting essentially of' to overcome examiner rejections, explore the ramifications: closed or partially closed phrases can narrow claim scope and cause unintended non-infringement. Consider consulting counsel to weigh prosecution benefits versus future enforcement risks.
